title: Safety Is Designed Before Anyone Arrives on Site
summary: Construction safety is decided long before the first worker arrives: by who you hire, what you require in the contract, and what the plan says about the hazards that kill people most often. This lesson covers OSHA's Focus Four hazards, the idea of a controlling employer on a multi-employer site, the site-specific safety plan, the job hazard analysis and how to prequalify contractors on safety.
body:
Most serious construction injuries come from a small number of known hazards, and the owner's leverage over them is greatest before the job starts. Hire for safety, write it into the contract, and insist on a plan that names the hazards on your site, not on a generic one.

Recall

Q. In Canadian tender law, what is Contract A?

A. The preliminary contract formed between an owner and each compliant bidder when a formal tender is submitted, which can carry duties such as treating bidders fairly and not accepting a non-compliant bid.

Q. Why keep escalation and allowances off the contingency line?

A. Because escalation is a forecast of price movement and allowances are placeholders, while contingency is for what you do not know. Merged, they make contingency look larger than it is.

Q. What is a take-out commitment?

A. A permanent lender's promise to repay the construction loan with a longer-term loan once stated conditions, such as completion and a level of income, are met.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you have worked in operations where a mistake could kill someone, so you already know that safety is a system, not a slogan. Construction is the same, with one difference that matters for a developer: the people at risk mostly do not work for you, yet the decisions that protect them, who is hired, how much time and money the job has, what the contract requires, are largely yours. A serious injury on your site is first a human tragedy, and then a legal, financial and reputational event for every party involved, including the owner.

The Focus Four: where the harm concentrates

The United States Occupational Safety and Health Administration, known as OSHA, groups the leading causes of construction deaths into what it calls the Focus Four: falls, struck-by, caught-in or caught-between, and electrocution. Falls from height are consistently among the largest causes. Struck-by covers being hit by falling objects, swinging loads or moving vehicles. Caught-in or between covers trench collapses and being crushed by equipment. Electrocution covers contact with live overhead lines and energised equipment. The federal construction safety standards are in Title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Part 1926. Verify the current text, and whether a state plan applies, against the primary source before you rely on it.

The professional framing: because the harm concentrates, so should the controls. A plan that spends equal effort on every hazard is diluted. A plan that names your fall exposures, your crane lifts, your excavations and your power lines, and says exactly how each is controlled, is the plan that saves lives.

Applied example, hypothetical. A six-month podium-and-frame residential job. Its Focus Four exposures are open edges and floor openings during framing, a mobile crane lifting trusses over a public sidewalk, a 3-metre-deep utility trench, and an overhead distribution line along one boundary. Four hazards, four named controls: guardrails and covers installed before edges are exposed, a lift plan with an exclusion zone, a trench protective system designed for the soil, and a de-energisation or clearance agreement with the utility before any equipment works near the line.

Who is responsible: the multi-employer site

A building site has many employers: the general contractor, dozens of subcontractors, suppliers and the owner's own staff. OSHA's multi-employer citation policy describes four roles an employer can play for a given hazard: the creating employer, who caused it; the exposing employer, whose own workers are exposed to it; the correcting employer, responsible for fixing it; and the controlling employer, with general supervisory authority over the site, including the power to correct or require others to correct. More than one employer can be cited for the same hazard. How this applies to an owner depends on how much control the owner actually exercises, and courts and review bodies have treated the question in different ways; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

The practical lesson for you as owner: control is a fact, not a title. If your representative directs how work is done, rather than what the result must be, you may be taking on the role of a controlling employer for that hazard. The disciplined owner requires a strong safety programme from the general contractor, monitors it, and uses contract rights to enforce it, without directing the trades' means and methods.

Say that out loud now.

Falls, struck-by, caught-in, electrocution. Control is a fact, not a title.

The site-specific safety plan and the job hazard analysis

A site-specific safety plan is the general contractor's written plan for this site: its hazards, the controls, emergency procedures, responsibilities, training, inspections and how subcontractors are brought in. Site-specific means it names this site's crane, this site's trench, this site's hospital route. A plan copied from another job, with the wrong address in the emergency section, is a warning sign about the whole safety culture.

A job hazard analysis, sometimes called a job safety analysis, breaks one task into steps, identifies the hazard in each step and sets the control, before the task starts. Example: setting steel beams. Step one, rigging the beam: hazard, a failed sling; control, inspected rigging rated for the load. Step two, lifting: hazard, a load over workers; control, an exclusion zone and tag lines. Step three, connecting: hazard, a fall from the beam; control, a tie-off point and fall arrest before stepping out. The value is not the form; it is the conversation among the crew who will do the work.

Prequalifying contractors on safety

Before a contractor bids, ask for its injury rates over several years, its experience modification rate where workers' compensation uses one, any regulatory citations and how they were resolved, its written safety programme, the name and credentials of its safety lead, and how it manages its own subcontractors. Day 5 shows how to read the numbers. A low price from a contractor with a poor record is a cost you have not yet been billed for.

How the best do it

Leading contractors treat safety as a line of the schedule, not an overlay on it. Safety planning is built into each phase's start-up meeting, pre-task planning happens daily at crew level, near misses are reported and analysed without blame, and senior leaders walk the site and stop work themselves when they see danger. A small developer can copy the part that costs nothing: require a pre-task plan before every high-risk activity, read a sample yourself every visit, and make it known that anyone may stop unsafe work without penalty.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: safety costs, fines and settlements can be treated differently for tax, and penalties are often not deductible; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a serious injury can bring regulatory, civil and in some systems criminal exposure to more than one party. Banking: a fatality or a stop-work order delays draws and can trigger default provisions. Governance: record how safety is reported to you and what you do with the report. Estate: personal liability claims can reach individuals; your estate plan should know your exposures. Exit: a site with a serious incident record can follow the asset and the developer's name into the next deal.

Professional sign-off required: a qualified safety professional, on the site-specific safety plan; a lawyer, on the owner's role and the contract's safety provisions.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating safety as the contractor's problem and then setting a price and schedule that make it impossible. The control is safety prequalification, contract requirements for a site-specific plan and pre-task planning, a realistic schedule, and monitoring without taking over the contractor's methods.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reads the safety plan's table of contents, sees that every heading is present, and approves it. Open it at the emergency section and the fall protection section. If they do not describe your site, the plan was not written for it.

Callback

In Week 52, Marco taught prequalification as the step that makes the lowest price a real option. Safety is the clearest case: a contractor that cannot show a safety record you would accept is not a real option at any price, because the cost of its failure lands on people first and on your project second.

Recap

The Focus Four, falls, struck-by, caught-in and electrocution, concentrate the harm, so concentrate the controls. On a multi-employer site, control is a fact, and an owner who directs methods can take on responsibility. Insist on a truly site-specific safety plan, task-level hazard analysis and safety prequalification.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: the Willow Island cooling tower collapse of 1978.
checklist: I can name my site's Focus Four exposures and the control for each.
The contract requires a site-specific safety plan before mobilisation.
I have read the plan's emergency and fall protection sections myself.
The contract requires a job hazard analysis before every high-risk task.
I prequalify contractors on injury rates, citations and their safety programme.
My representatives monitor safety and use contract rights without directing methods.
Anyone on site may stop unsafe work without penalty, and the contract says so.
A safety professional and a lawyer have reviewed my safety provisions.
head: Field checklist
speak: Construction safety is decided before anyone arrives on site, by who I hire, what the contract requires and how much time the job has. OSHA groups the leading causes of construction deaths into the Focus Four: falls, struck-by, caught-in or between, and electrocution. Because the harm concentrates, the controls must too, so my plan names this site's edges, crane lifts, trenches and power lines and the control for each. A site has many employers, and OSHA's multi-employer policy recognises the creating, exposing, correcting and controlling employer. Control is a fact, not a title: if my people direct how the work is done, I may take on responsibility. So I require a strong programme from the general contractor and enforce it through the contract. I insist on a truly site-specific safety plan, a job hazard analysis before high-risk tasks, and safety prequalification. A low price from a contractor with a poor record is a bill I have not yet received.
terms: Focus Four — OSHA's grouping of the leading causes of construction deaths: falls, struck-by, caught-in or between, and electrocution.
Controlling employer — under OSHA's multi-employer policy, an employer with general supervisory authority over a site, including the power to correct hazards or require others to.
Job hazard analysis — a written breakdown of one task into steps, with the hazard and control for each step, prepared before the task begins.

hostile.q: You are the owner, not the contractor. Why should safety on this site be any of your concern?
hostile.a: Because the decisions that make a site safe or unsafe start with me: who I hire, the time and money I give the job, and what the contract requires. A serious incident delays the project, can trigger default provisions in the loan, and can expose more than one party to liability. So I prequalify on safety, require a site-specific plan and pre-task planning, and monitor through the contract. I do not direct the trades' methods; I make sure the contractor has the means, the plan and the obligation to do it right.

title: Willow Island, 1978: When Fresh Concrete Was Asked to Carry Too Much
summary: On 27 April 1978, a cooling tower under construction at Willow Island, West Virginia, partially collapsed and 51 construction workers on its scaffolding were killed. Ford and Cole take the case through seven forensic steps, focusing on what any owner can control: proving that a structure can carry a load before the load is applied.
body:
At Willow Island, the scaffolding that held 51 workers was anchored into concrete that was not yet strong enough to carry it. No contract, schedule or production target can be allowed to decide when a structure is strong enough; only a measured result can.

Recall

Q. On the week 52 numbers, what was the trade budget behind a 15,900,000 dollar guaranteed maximum price?

A. 13,000,000 dollars, after dividing out 6 percent fee and insurance, subtracting 1,480,000 dollars of general conditions and dividing out a 4 percent contractor's contingency.

Q. What was Rule 51?

A. Report the forecast final cost, in the dollars you will actually pay, every month to the people funding the project, and never let a published estimate leave out a cost you know you will pay.

Q. What is a maturity gap in exit financing?

A. The period between the construction loan's maturity and the date the project can actually be refinanced or sold, which must be bridged or the loan falls into default.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Cole joins me because this case shaped how construction safety is regulated and litigated. It is also the clearest example I know of a structural question, is the concrete strong enough yet, being answered by the clock instead of by a test. You will face that question in a smaller form on every concrete building you build.

A note on facts. The collapse is real and was investigated by the United States government's National Bureau of Standards and by OSHA. The broad sequence below is well documented; I give only the facts I am confident of, and where I describe decisions and incentives, treat it as my analysis and verify specifics against the published investigation before you rely on them.

1. Timeline

Through the 1970s, a power station at Willow Island, near St. Marys, West Virginia, was being expanded, including a large hyperbolic concrete cooling tower. The tower shell was built in lifts: a ring of concrete was placed, and the scaffolding and formwork system was then raised and anchored into the concrete below it to form the next ring. On 27 April 1978, as concrete was being raised and placed at the top, the most recently placed section and the scaffolding attached to it failed and fell to the ground inside the tower. All 51 workers on the scaffold were killed. It is among the deadliest construction accidents in the history of the United States.

2. Key decisions

The decision that mattered most was to raise the system and load it from concrete placed only the day before, without confirming that the concrete had reached the strength needed to carry the scaffold, the workers and the next placement. Behind that were decisions about the climbing system itself, its anchorage into young concrete, and the pace of the work.

3. Assumptions

The operation assumed that the concrete would gain enough strength within the normal cycle, whatever the conditions. Concrete gains strength with time and temperature, and on cool days it gains it more slowly. An assumption that is true on a warm day can be false on a cold one, and an operation that does not test cannot tell the difference.

4. Incentives

A climbing-form operation on a tall shell is a repeating cycle, and every cycle has a production target. A crew, a supervisor and a contractor all have reasons to keep the cycle moving: cost, schedule and the momentum of a repetitive task done many times before without incident. None of those incentives is wicked. All of them push toward loading the structure as early as possible, and none of them measures whether it is ready.

Say that out loud now.

The clock does not decide when concrete is strong enough. A test does.

5. Warning signs ignored

In general terms: young concrete supporting a heavy, occupied temporary structure; cooler conditions that slow strength gain; a repetitive cycle with no hold point for strength verification; and a temporary works design whose assumptions about concrete strength were not tied to field results. These are exactly the signals that a modern quality plan converts into a hold point: a step at which work stops until a named person confirms a measured result.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the moment the system was raised and loaded onto concrete that had not been confirmed strong enough. Before that, a test result or a delay of a day would have prevented the collapse. After it, there was nothing anyone on the scaffold could do.

7. Root cause

The root cause was that a structural readiness decision, loading young concrete, was made by schedule and habit rather than by verified strength. The temporary works, the scaffold and its anchorage, depended on the permanent works having reached a strength that nobody measured before relying on it.

Cole's view: what followed, and what it means for owners

After the collapse, OSHA issued citations to the contractors involved, and the case became part of the record that informed later regulation of concrete construction and formwork. The exact citations, penalties and later rule changes should be verified against the primary sources before you cite them. The point for an owner is wider than any one rule. On a multi-employer site, a temporary works failure can involve the designer of the temporary works, the contractor erecting it, the concrete supplier and testing agency, and whoever controls the site. An owner who pressures the cycle, or who directs the sequence, can find itself in that chain. Your protection is to require a temporary works design, a hold point on strength, and a testing regime, and never to push the cycle against a test result.

What this means on an ordinary building

You will probably never build a cooling tower, but you will strip formwork, remove shores, load slabs with stored materials and hang scaffolds from new structure. Each is the same question in miniature. On a hypothetical mid-rise, the formwork contractor wants to strip a slab after a set number of days and move the forms up. The disciplined answer is to ask what strength the temporary works designer requires before stripping and reshoring, how that strength will be shown, by field-cured cylinders or by a maturity method that estimates strength from the concrete's temperature history, and who signs the release. If those three answers exist in writing, the cycle can run fast safely. If they do not, the cycle is running on hope.

The prevention

Rule 53: Never let a structure, permanent or temporary, carry a load until a measured result shows it can; write that hold point into the plan, and never let schedule override it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a repetitive cycle in which a structural assumption has held many times and so stops being checked. The control is a hold point, a named person with authority to release it, and a measured result, such as field-cured cylinder breaks or maturity measurements, before any load is applied.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats temporary works, scaffolds, formwork, shoring and reshoring, as the contractor's housekeeping. They are structures, they carry people, and they need a design and a check like any other structure.

Callback

In Week 6 and again in the Week 21 case, Ford took the Hyatt Regency walkways of 1981, where a change to a connection was never confirmed by the engineer who owned the design. Willow Island is the same failure in a different form: a load path that depended on an assumption nobody verified. In both, the people who died were standing on a structure whose safety had been assumed rather than proven.

Recap

On 27 April 1978, a cooling tower under construction at Willow Island partially collapsed and 51 workers were killed, when the scaffold system was loaded from concrete placed the day before that was not yet strong enough. The root cause was a readiness decision made by schedule rather than by test.

Rule 53: Never let a structure, permanent or temporary, carry a load until a measured result shows it can; write that hold point into the plan, and never let schedule override it.

Next: Roman on The Money: what safety and its failures cost the project, the lender and the developer.
checklist: Every temporary works item, scaffold, formwork and shoring, has a design by a qualified person.
The quality plan has a hold point before any load is applied to new concrete.
A named person with authority releases each structural hold point.
Strength is confirmed by a measured result, such as field-cured cylinders or maturity readings.
I never press the contractor's cycle against a test result.
Cold-weather concreting has its own plan for slower strength gain.
My representatives monitor hold points without directing the contractor's methods.
head: Field checklist
speak: On 27 April 1978, at Willow Island in West Virginia, a cooling tower under construction partially collapsed, and the 51 workers on its scaffolding were killed. The tower was built in lifts: concrete was placed, and the scaffold and forms were then raised and anchored into the concrete below to form the next ring. The section that failed had been placed only the day before and was not yet strong enough to carry the scaffold, the workers and the next placement. The root cause was that a structural readiness decision was made by the clock and habit of a repeating cycle, not by a measured result. Concrete gains strength more slowly in cool conditions, and an operation that does not test cannot tell. For an owner, the lessons are to require a temporary works design, a hold point on strength and testing, and never to push the cycle against a test. Rule 53: never let a structure carry a load until a measured result shows it can.
terms: Temporary works — structures used only during construction, such as scaffolds, formwork, shoring and reshoring, which carry real loads and need design.
Hold point — a defined step in a quality or safety plan at which work must stop until a named person confirms a required result.
Field-cured cylinder — a concrete test specimen kept in site conditions, so its strength reflects the concrete actually in the structure.

hostile.q: Your contractor wants to strip the forms a day early to recover the schedule. You are behind. Why are you standing in the way?
hostile.a: I am not standing in the way of the schedule; I am standing in the way of loading concrete we have not proven is ready. Our plan has a hold point: the forms come off and the next load goes on when the field-cured cylinders, or the maturity readings, show the strength the temporary works design requires, released by the engineer named in the plan. If the results are there tomorrow, we strip tomorrow. If they are not, we find the time somewhere else.

rule: Rule 53: Never let a structure, permanent or temporary, carry a load until a measured result shows it can; write that hold point into the plan, and never let schedule override it.

title: What an Incident Costs: Shutdowns, Premiums and the Lender's Clock
summary: Safety is first a duty to people, but a developer also has to understand its money. This lesson traces a hypothetical serious incident through a stop-work period, interest and overhead, delayed income, insurance and the loan documents, shows how a contractor's safety record is priced into its bid, and closes with Warrick's Wealth Ledger on personal exposure.
body:
A serious incident is a human tragedy before it is anything else. It is also a financial event whose largest costs are usually uninsured: weeks of interest and overhead while the site is stopped, income that starts late, and a lender who now watches every draw.

Recall

Q. What should you do if a bidder offers you a personal benefit during an award?

A. Refuse at once, return to the business at hand, and write a note to the file, telling partners or the lender if your agreements require it.

Q. Why does a 10 percent cost overrun hit equity harder than 10 percent?

A. Because the loan is usually fixed at closing, so the whole overrun is funded with equity; on the week 51 numbers, profit fell 37 percent.

Q. Why does the exit cap rate matter so much to a development's return?

A. Because the sale or refinance value is income divided by the exit cap rate, so a small rise in that rate at exit cuts value, and the equity's return, sharply.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, I am going to talk about money in a lesson that follows a case where 51 people died. I do that on purpose. Developers who think safety is only a cost tend to spend too little on it, and developers who think it is only a moral question tend to leave it to others. It is both, and understanding its money is part of taking it seriously.

The two kinds of cost

The direct costs of an injury, medical treatment and wage replacement, are largely carried by workers' compensation or similar insurance schemes, depending on the jurisdiction. The indirect costs are mostly not insured: work stopped while the scene is investigated, regulatory inspection, repairs to damaged work and equipment, time lost by supervisors and the crew, recruitment and retraining, legal costs, fines and penalties, and harm to reputation. Practitioners often say indirect costs exceed direct costs by a large multiple. The multiple varies widely by study and by incident, so do not rely on any single figure; the direction is what matters.

A hypothetical stop-work, priced

A serious incident on a mid-rise job leads to a three-week stoppage of most site work while the incident is investigated and controls are re-verified. The construction loan has 15,000,000 dollars drawn at 7 percent interest a year.

Interest: 15,000,000 times 0.07 divided by 52 weeks is about 20,192 dollars a week, so three weeks is about 60,577 dollars. General conditions, the contractor's site overheads that continue while work is stopped, are 30,000 dollars a week, about 90,000 dollars for three weeks, recoverable by the contractor or not depending on the contract and the cause. The building's stabilised net operating income will be 1,200,000 dollars a year, about 23,077 dollars a week; a three-week slip in completion delays about 69,231 dollars of income. Before legal costs, fines, repairs or any effect on the lender, the stoppage costs roughly 60,577 plus 90,000 plus 69,231, about 220,000 dollars.

Compare that with prevention. A dedicated, competent safety lead for a year, proper edge protection, and time in the schedule for pre-task planning cost money too, but they are known, budgeted and small next to the downside. That is not a promise that spending prevents every incident; it is the arithmetic of a priced risk.

Say that out loud now.

The insured cost is the small one. The stopped site, the late income and the lender's clock are mine.

How safety is priced into the bid

In the United States, many workers' compensation premiums are adjusted by an experience modification rate: a factor comparing a contractor's own claims history with that expected for its trade and size. A rate below 1.0 means a better than expected history and a lower premium; above 1.0 means a worse one and a higher premium. Canadian provinces run their own workers' compensation systems, many with experience rating of their own. Verify how the rate is calculated in the relevant jurisdiction before you rely on it.

The money point: a contractor with a poor record pays more for insurance, and that cost is in its price, or, if it is not, its margin is thinner than its competitors'. Either way, the safety record is telling you something about the bid. Applied example, hypothetical: two bids within 1 percent of each other, one from a contractor whose rate has been well below 1.0 for years and one from a contractor whose rate has risen above 1.0. The second contractor's price may be squeezing its margin, and a squeezed margin is where shortcuts come from.

When the owner buys the insurance

On some larger projects, the owner buys one insurance programme covering all contractors on the site, called an owner-controlled insurance programme, instead of each contractor buying its own. A contractor-controlled version also exists. Week 79 covers them properly. The money point for today is that when you buy the programme, the site's safety performance flows straight into your own premiums and claims, so the incentive to run a safe site moves to you. Whether such a programme is available, sensible or even permitted for a project of your size and location is a question for a broker and a lawyer; do not assume it.

What the lender sees

Construction loan documents commonly require the borrower to comply with applicable law, to keep the project insured, and to notify the lender of material adverse events. A fatality, a major regulatory stop-work order or an uninsured liability can touch all three. The lender's monitor will report the stoppage, the draw schedule will slip, and the in-balance test will absorb the extra interest and overhead. The exact consequences depend on your loan documents; read them before construction starts, not after an incident. Your lender's question will be simple: what happened, what has changed, and what does it do to cost to complete.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Warrick's point for your personal balance sheet is that insurance has limits and exclusions, and that fines and penalties are often not insurable at all. In some jurisdictions, serious failures of safety duty can expose individuals, including officers and directors, to prosecution, not only the company. The protection is not to hold back from the project but to make sure your governance is real: that safety is reported to you, that you act on what you hear, and that the record shows it. Ask your adviser what insurance you and your entities carry against liability claims arising from your projects, and what it excludes. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a budget and schedule so tight that the contractor's only room is in safety. The control is a realistic programme with time for planning, safety prequalification that reads the record behind the price, and a budget line for safety you will not cut to close a gap elsewhere.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner looks at the insurance policy, sees that injuries are covered, and concludes that the financial risk is handled. The insured part is the smaller part.

Callback

In Week 52, Priya priced a month at the end of construction at interest plus income not yet earned. A safety stoppage is the same arithmetic arriving without warning, and Rule 52 applies here too: transferring the work to a contractor does not transfer the delay off your calendar.

Recap

Direct injury costs are largely insured; indirect costs, a stopped site, investigation, legal costs and late income, are largely not. A hypothetical three-week stoppage cost about 220,000 dollars before fines or repairs. Experience rating prices a contractor's record into its bid, and the loan documents decide how an incident touches your financing.

Next: REGA on The Rules: OSHA Part 1926, the multi-employer policy and how Canada and Guyana approach construction safety law.
checklist: I can price one week of stoppage: interest, general conditions and delayed income.
I know which incident costs are insured and which are not.
I read each bidder's experience rating and injury history beside its price.
My budget has a safety line I will not cut to close a gap elsewhere.
I know what my loan documents require me to report after a serious incident.
My programme includes time for pre-task planning and safety inspections.
I know what liability insurance I and my entities carry, and what it excludes.
head: Field checklist
speak: A serious incident is a tragedy first, and also a financial event whose largest costs are usually uninsured. Direct costs, treatment and wage replacement, are largely carried by workers' compensation. Indirect costs mostly are not: a stopped site, investigation, repairs, legal costs, fines and reputation. On a hypothetical job with 15,000,000 dollars drawn at 7 percent, a three-week stoppage costs about 60,000 dollars of interest, 90,000 of site overhead and about 69,000 of delayed income, roughly 220,000 dollars before fines or repairs. Safety is also priced into bids: in the United States, an experience modification rate below 1.0 means a better record and a lower premium, above 1.0 a worse one. A contractor with a poor record is either charging me for it or squeezing its margin, and a squeezed margin is where shortcuts come from. Finally, my loan documents decide how an incident touches my financing, so I read them before construction starts.
terms: Indirect costs of an incident — the largely uninsured costs that follow an injury, such as stoppage, investigation, repairs, legal costs and lost productivity.
Experience modification rate — a factor used in many United States workers' compensation systems comparing a firm's claims history with the expected history for its trade and size.
Material adverse event — an event that significantly harms a borrower or project, which loan documents often require the borrower to report.

hostile.q: You chose a contractor that was half a percent more expensive. Your investors want to know why you didn't take the cheaper bid.
hostile.a: Because the cheaper bid came from a contractor whose experience rating has risen above 1.0 and whose injury rates have worsened for three years, while the one we chose has a long record well below expected. Half a percent on this job is a small fraction of what a single three-week stoppage would cost us in interest, overhead and delayed income, before fines or reputation. I will share the prequalification comparison so the investors can see the record behind each price.

title: The Safety Rulebook: OSHA Part 1926, Shared Duties and Two Systems
summary: How construction safety law is organised: the American federal construction standards in OSHA Part 1926, the general duty that sits behind them, the multi-employer citation policy, and what an inspection and citation involve. The lesson closes with a conceptual comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach construction safety law.
body:
Construction safety law works in two layers: specific standards that say how named hazards must be controlled, and a general duty that catches hazards the standards do not name. On a multi-employer site, more than one firm can be responsible for the same hazard, and the owner is not automatically outside that circle.

Recall

Q. What evidence should a procurement award file be able to produce?

A. The tender rules, the bid opening record, the levelling sheet, the initialled scope list, signed conflict-of-interest declarations, the names of at least two evaluators, and file notes of any unusual approach.

Q. In common law systems, does a contract end because performing it became much more expensive?

A. Generally not. Courts usually hold parties to their bargain; the classic English example is Davis Contractors against Fareham, decided in 1956.

Q. What usually has to happen before a take-out lender funds?

A. The conditions in its commitment must be met, typically completion, occupancy approvals, a stated level of leasing or income, and clean title, by a stated date.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Duke taught the system and Roman priced its failure. Today I give you the rulebook in outline, so you can read a safety plan, a contract clause or a regulator's notice and know where it sits. I will not tell you what any rule requires on your site; that depends on the jurisdiction, the edition and the facts, and a qualified safety professional and a lawyer must confirm it.

Layer one: the specific standards

In the United States, the federal construction safety standards are in Title 29 of the Code of Federal Regulations, Part 1926, divided into subparts by topic. Among them are subparts on fall protection, scaffolds, excavations, electrical work, cranes and derricks, and concrete and masonry construction. Each sets requirements for a hazard: for example, the fall protection subpart sets the conditions under which employees working at height must be protected, and the methods that count as protection. The trigger heights, distances and specifications in these standards are exactly the kind of figure you must verify against the current text, and against any state plan that applies, before you rely on it. Many states run their own approved occupational safety plans, which must be at least as effective as the federal programme and can be stricter.

Applied example, hypothetical. Your general contractor's safety plan says that fall protection will be provided "where required by regulation." That sentence is useless. A good plan says which edges and openings on your site are exposed, which method protects each, guardrails, covers, safety nets or personal fall arrest, who installs and inspects it, and when. The regulation sets the floor; the plan shows how this site meets it.

Layer two: the general duty

Behind the specific standards sits the general duty in the federal Occupational Safety and Health Act, which requires employers to keep their workplaces free of recognised hazards likely to cause death or serious physical harm. It is used where no specific standard addresses a hazard. Verify its text and how it is applied before you rely on it. The practical consequence: "there is no rule about it" is not a defence for a recognised hazard.

Say that out loud now.

The standards set the floor. The general duty catches what the standards do not name. "There is no rule" is not a defence.

The multi-employer policy, inspections and citations

As Duke taught, OSHA's multi-employer citation policy recognises creating, exposing, correcting and controlling employers, and more than one can be cited for the same hazard. A controlling employer is generally expected to exercise reasonable care to prevent and detect violations, with the level of care depending on its role and expertise. How far this reaches an owner turns on the control the owner actually exercises; it has been contested, and you need specific legal advice on your arrangement.

An inspection can follow a complaint, a referral, a serious incident, or a programmed selection. Inspectors may review the site, the written programme and records, and interview workers. A citation names the standard alleged to be violated, a classification such as serious or willful, a proposed penalty and an abatement date by which the hazard must be corrected. Employers can contest citations through a formal process with time limits. Penalty amounts are adjusted over time; never quote one from memory, and verify against the primary source.

Applied example, hypothetical. An inspector cites the framing subcontractor for unprotected edges as the exposing and creating employer, and the general contractor as the controlling employer for failing to detect and correct it. The owner's representative had issued a written instruction telling the framer the order in which to install the edge protection. That instruction is the kind of fact that brings an owner into the question. The better instruction would have been a requirement on the general contractor: "edge protection installed before any edge is exposed, per the site-specific safety plan."

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

Treat this as a conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source before you rely on any of it. In Canada, occupational health and safety is mainly provincial, so each province and territory has its own act and construction regulations, with federal law covering federally regulated workplaces. Several provinces assign duties by role; Ontario, for example, uses the concept of a constructor, the party with overall responsibility for a project, and an owner who takes on that role takes on its duties. After the Westray mine explosion in Nova Scotia in 1992, Parliament amended the Criminal Code to set out a legal duty on those who direct work to take reasonable steps to prevent bodily harm, with the amendments in force from 2004. Guyana has an occupational safety and health statute administered by its labour authorities, which places duties on employers and others at workplaces [unverified — confirm independently]. In both countries, international lenders funding a project often add their own environmental, health and safety standards on top of local law, and those can be stricter.

Professional sign-off required: a qualified safety professional, on compliance with the applicable standards; a lawyer, on the owner's role and exposure in the relevant jurisdiction.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an owner who takes on control without realising it, by directing methods and sequences, while assuming the contractor alone carries the legal duty. The control is contracts that place safety responsibility clearly on the general contractor, owner's instructions written as requirements for outcomes, and legal advice on the owner's role in each jurisdiction.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes the rules are the same everywhere because a well-known federal standard exists. A state plan, a province or another country may be stricter, may assign duties differently, and may criminalise what elsewhere is a civil matter. The second beginner's mistake is to treat a citation as a fine to be paid and filed. The abatement date is the real obligation, and a hazard still present when the inspector returns is a far more serious matter than the first finding.

Callback

In Week 21, LEX and Omar taught that limited liability protects a shareholder from a company's debts, but does not protect a person from liability for his own acts. Safety law is where that distinction is sharpest: the corporate structure may limit financial exposure, but an individual who directs work can carry duties, and in some systems criminal duties, personally.

Recap

OSHA Part 1926 sets specific construction standards by subpart, and a general duty covers recognised hazards the standards do not name. The multi-employer policy lets more than one firm be cited for one hazard, and owners who exercise control can be drawn in. In Canada safety law is mainly provincial, with Criminal Code duties after Westray; Guyana has its own statute, to be verified.

Next: Duke on The Numbers: injury rates, experience ratings and reading a contractor's safety record.
checklist: I know which safety regime applies: federal, state plan, province or another country.
The safety plan shows how each named hazard on my site meets the standard, not just that it will.
I treat recognised hazards as covered even where no specific standard names them.
My contracts place primary safety responsibility clearly on the general contractor.
My representatives write instructions as required outcomes, not as methods.
I know the contest process and time limits if a citation arrives.
I have legal advice on the owner's safety role in each jurisdiction I build in.
head: Field checklist
speak: Construction safety law has two layers. In the United States, Part 1926 of the federal regulations sets specific standards by subpart, for fall protection, scaffolds, excavations, electrical work, cranes and concrete. Behind them, the general duty requires employers to keep workplaces free of recognised hazards likely to cause death or serious harm, so no rule about it is not a defence. I verify every height, distance and penalty against the current text and any state plan. On a multi-employer site, more than one firm can be cited for one hazard, and an owner who directs methods can be drawn in, so my instructions state outcomes, not methods. A citation names the standard, a classification, a proposed penalty and an abatement date, and it can be contested within time limits. In Canada, safety law is mainly provincial, with Criminal Code duties added after the Westray disaster. Guyana has its own statute, which I would verify before relying on it.
terms: General duty — the obligation in the federal Occupational Safety and Health Act for employers to keep workplaces free of recognised hazards likely to cause death or serious harm.
Abatement date — the date set in a citation by which the cited hazard must be corrected.
Constructor — in some Canadian provinces, notably Ontario, the party with overall responsibility for a construction project and the safety duties that go with it.

hostile.q: The regulator has cited the general contractor as controlling employer and is asking about your representative's instructions to the framer. Aren't you exposed?
hostile.a: I may be, and I am taking it seriously. I have asked counsel to review every instruction my representative issued and the contract's allocation of safety responsibility. Going forward, my team will issue requirements for outcomes to the general contractor, not methods to subcontractors. I will cooperate fully with the inspection, and the general contractor will abate the hazard by the date given, with my monitoring confirming it.

title: Reading a Safety Record: Incident Rates, Hours and Small Samples
summary: A worked calculation that turns three hypothetical contractors' injury logs into comparable rates. Step by step: the total recordable incident rate, the rate of cases involving days away or restricted work, the effect of small samples, experience ratings, the expected number of injuries on your own project, and the leading indicators that predict what the rates will show.
body:
Raw injury counts cannot be compared between contractors of different sizes; rates per hours worked can. Convert every record to a rate, check the sample is large enough to mean anything, and then ask for the leading indicators that tell you what next year's rate will be.

Recall

Q. Name the Focus Four.

A. Falls, struck-by, caught-in or caught-between, and electrocution: OSHA's grouping of the leading causes of construction deaths.

Q. What does a cost performance index of 0.909 mean?

A. That each dollar spent has bought about 91 cents of budgeted work; it is earned value divided by actual cost.

Q. How is debt yield calculated?

A. Net operating income divided by the loan amount, expressed as a percentage; lenders use it as a test of loan size that does not depend on interest rates or cap rates.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a contractor's safety record arrives as a page of numbers in a prequalification package. Most owners glance at it. Today you learn to read it the way an experienced safety professional does, in about ten minutes, with a calculator. The method is the same discipline Quincy used on earned value: convert raw figures to a comparable rate, then test what the rate can and cannot tell you.

Step 1: the recordable incident rate

A recordable injury, broadly, is a work-related injury or illness that meets the recording criteria, for example one needing medical treatment beyond first aid, days away from work, or restricted work. The exact criteria are set by the recordkeeping rules in each jurisdiction; verify them against the primary source before you rely on them.

The total recordable incident rate converts a count into a rate per 100 full-time workers for a year. The formula is: number of recordable cases, times 200,000, divided by total hours worked. The 200,000 is 100 workers times 40 hours a week times 50 weeks a year.

Three hypothetical contractors report last year's figures.

Contractor X: 6 recordable cases in 600,000 hours. Rate: 6 times 200,000 is 1,200,000, divided by 600,000, equals 2.0.

Contractor Y: 4 recordable cases in 100,000 hours. Rate: 4 times 200,000 is 800,000, divided by 100,000, equals 8.0.

Contractor Z: 0 recordable cases in 40,000 hours. Rate: 0.

By count, Y looks better than X, with 4 cases against 6. By rate, Y is four times worse, because X worked six times as many hours.

Say that out loud now.

Cases times 200,000, divided by hours. Never compare counts.

Step 2: the severity rate

The total rate counts every recordable case alike. A second rate counts only cases serious enough to involve days away from work, restricted work or job transfer, often abbreviated DART. Same formula, different count.

Contractor X had 3 such cases: 3 times 200,000 divided by 600,000 equals 1.0. Contractor Y had 2: 2 times 200,000 divided by 100,000 equals 4.0. So half of X's cases were serious, and half of Y's. The severity rate confirms the picture rather than changing it.

ContractorHoursRecordable casesTotal rateSerious casesSeverity rate
X600,00062.031.0
Y100,00048.024.0
Z40,00000.000.0

Step 3: the small-sample trap

Contractor Z's perfect zero looks best. Test it: if Z had had just one recordable case in its 40,000 hours, its rate would be 1 times 200,000 divided by 40,000, which is 5.0. A single event moves Z from best to second worst. Its zero is real, but it is not strong evidence, because 40,000 hours is about 20 full-time workers for a year.

The cure is more hours: ask for three to five years of data, and add them up. Suppose Z worked 40,000, 45,000 and 35,000 hours over three years, a total of 120,000, with 0, 2 and 1 cases, a total of 3. Three-year rate: 3 times 200,000 divided by 120,000 equals 5.0. The single good year was not the pattern.

Do the same for X: suppose its rates over three years were 2.4, 2.1 and 2.0. That is a large sample and an improving trend, which is the strongest signal in the table.

Step 4: experience rating beside the rates

Where the bidders' workers' compensation uses an experience modification rate, put it beside the incident rates. Suppose X's is 0.82, Y's 1.25 and Z's 0.95. X's is below 1.0, meaning a better claims history than expected for its trade and size, and consistent with its rates. Y's above 1.0 is consistent with its high rates. When a contractor's rates look good but its experience rating is poor, ask why: the rates may be under-recorded. Verify how the rating is calculated in the relevant jurisdiction before you rely on it.

Step 5: what the rates mean for your project

Estimate your project's hours. A 12-month job averaging 40 workers on site, each working 40 hours a week for 50 weeks, is 40 times 40 times 50, which is 80,000 hours. Expected recordable cases at a rate of 2.0: 80,000 times 2.0 divided by 200,000, which is 0.8. At a rate of 8.0: 80,000 times 8.0 divided by 200,000, which is 3.2. The difference between the two contractors is roughly two to three additional recordable injuries on your project, about half of them serious enough to involve lost or restricted time. These are people, and each one carries the costs Roman priced on Day 3.

Step 6: leading indicators

Injury rates are lagging indicators: they count harm that has already happened. Leading indicators measure the activities that prevent it. Ask for them, and track them on your own job: the share of high-risk tasks with a completed job hazard analysis, the number of near misses reported per month, the number of site inspections completed against plan, and the time taken to close corrective actions. Hypothetical: 95 of 100 high-risk tasks started with a completed analysis, a 95 percent completion rate. A contractor that reports many near misses is usually not more dangerous; it is usually more honest.

Step 7: three questions when the numbers look wrong

First, whose hours are these? A general contractor that reports only its own direct employees' hours, and none of its subcontractors', can show a very different rate from one that reports the whole site. Ask which basis is used, and compare like with like. Second, how are cases recorded? A firm that moves injured workers to light duty to avoid a lost-time case can keep its severity rate low while its total rate stays high; a large gap between the two is worth a question. Third, what happened? Ask for a short description of the serious cases and what changed afterwards. A contractor that can tell you, specifically, what it learned from its last serious injury is usually safer than one with a cleaner page and nothing to say.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is trusting a low rate built on few hours or on poor recording. The control is several years of data added together, an experience rating beside the rates, and leading indicators that show the prevention activity behind the numbers.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner disqualifies any contractor with an injury and prefers the one reporting zero. Prefer the large sample, the improving trend and the honest near-miss reporting.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the outside view: judge a forecast against the record of similar cases, not against the story. A contractor's three-year rate is its reference class. One perfect year is a story; the sum of the hours is the evidence.

Recap

Rate equals cases times 200,000 divided by hours. X's 6 cases in 600,000 hours gave 2.0; Y's 4 in 100,000 gave 8.0; Z's zero in 40,000 hours would become 5.0 with one case, and its three-year rate was 5.0. On an 80,000-hour project, 2.0 implies 0.8 expected recordable cases and 8.0 implies 3.2. Read leading indicators beside the rates.

Next: Duke on The Room: the stop-work conversation with a superintendent who is behind schedule.
checklist: I convert every injury count into a rate per 200,000 hours.
I compare both the total recordable rate and the severity rate.
I ask for three to five years of data and add the hours together.
I test small samples by adding one case and recomputing.
I read the experience rating beside the incident rates.
I estimate my project's hours and the expected recordable cases at each bidder's rate.
I ask for leading indicators, including near-miss reporting and hazard analysis completion.
head: Field checklist
speak: I never compare injury counts, only rates. The total recordable incident rate is recordable cases times 200,000, divided by hours worked; the 200,000 is 100 full-time workers for a year. Hypothetical contractor X had 6 cases in 600,000 hours, a rate of 2.0. Contractor Y had 4 cases in 100,000 hours, a rate of 8.0, four times worse despite fewer cases. Contractor Z had zero in 40,000 hours, but one case would make it 5.0, and its three-year rate was 5.0, so its perfect year was not the pattern. I read the severity rate, for serious cases, and the experience rating beside them. Then I apply the rates to my project: 80,000 hours at 2.0 means about 0.8 expected recordable cases, and at 8.0 about 3.2. Finally, rates are lagging indicators, so I ask for leading ones, such as near-miss reports and hazard analyses completed, which show the prevention behind the numbers.
terms: Total recordable incident rate — the number of recordable work injuries and illnesses per 100 full-time workers for a year, equal to cases times 200,000 divided by hours worked.
Severity rate — here, the rate of cases involving days away from work, restricted work or job transfer, calculated with the same formula.
Leading indicator — a measure of prevention activity, such as near misses reported or hazard analyses completed, that predicts future safety performance.

hostile.q: Contractor Z reported zero injuries last year. You recommended X, which had six. Explain that to my investment committee.
hostile.a: Z's zero came from about 40,000 hours, roughly 20 workers for a year; one case would have made its rate 5.0, and over three years its rate is 5.0. X's six cases came from 600,000 hours, a rate of 2.0, improving for three years, with an experience rating well below 1.0 and strong near-miss reporting. On our 80,000-hour project, X's record implies under one expected recordable case. I will send the committee the three-year comparison.

title: The Stop-Work Conversation: Behind Schedule, at an Open Edge
summary: A realistic site walk where the owner sees workers at an unprotected slab edge on a job that is behind schedule, and the superintendent pushes back. The lesson gives the lines to say and never to say, the question behind each question, when to stay silent, how an owner acts without taking over the contractor's methods, and how to hold steady when the pressure is all toward keeping the work moving.
body:
When you see danger on your site, say so at once, to the person who controls the work, in plain words, and make sure work stops at that hazard until it is controlled. Then let the contractor fix it its way, and follow it up in writing.

Recall

Q. What was Rule 53?

A. Never let a structure, permanent or temporary, carry a load until a measured result shows it can; write that hold point into the plan, and never let schedule override it.

Q. In the week 51 cost meeting, why open with the forecast number?

A. Because whoever states the bad number first owns the conversation, while leading with explanations leaves the room wondering how bad it is.

Q. What should you bring to a refinancing meeting with a new lender?

A. The stabilised income with evidence behind it, the rent roll, the proposed loan size tested against coverage and debt yield, and the date the existing loan matures, so the lender sees the gap you need closed and how it is covered.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you have heard four lessons of theory this week. This one is about a single minute on a slab. In your power-grid work you have watched an operator decide, under pressure, whether to stop or carry on. The site version is the same moment, and the owner, who controls the money and the schedule, has more influence in it than almost anyone else.

The scene

A mid-rise frame, hypothetical, two weeks behind schedule. You are on a site walk with your owner's representative and the general contractor's superintendent. On level five, two framers are working near the slab edge. The perimeter guardrail has been taken down along about ten metres to land a bundle of studs, and neither worker is tied off. It is a five-storey drop.

You stop walking and speak to the superintendent, not to the framers.

"Those two men at the edge are not protected, and the guardrail is down. I need work at that edge to stop now, until it's protected. You decide how. I'll wait here."

That is three things: the hazard named exactly, the outcome you require, and the method left to the contractor. You speak to the person who controls the work, because shouting instructions to another employer's workers is both less effective and the kind of direction of methods REGA warned about on Day 4. If the danger were immediate and the superintendent were not beside you, you would warn the workers directly, because preventing a fall outranks every point of contract procedure.

The pushback

The superintendent says, "They're nearly done, it's ten more minutes, and we're two weeks behind. The guardrail goes back up after the bundle lands." You answer calmly.

"I understand the schedule, and I'll talk to you about the schedule afterwards. Not at this edge. Nothing about two weeks is worth a fall from five storeys."

The superintendent says, "Our safety plan allows controlled access zones for this." You answer: "Then show me the zone and its monitor. I don't see either. Until there is one, the edge stops."

Say that out loud now.

Name the hazard. State the outcome. Leave the method to them. Stay until it is done.

The lines to say

Say the hazard in concrete terms: "unprotected edge, guardrail removed, no tie-off." Say the outcome, not the method: "protected before work resumes," not "put the rail back on the third post." Say that you will wait: it shows the instruction is not a suggestion. Afterwards say, in writing, what you saw, the time, what was done and what you expect to change: "Please confirm by tomorrow how material landings at open edges will be planned so the edge stays protected."

The lines never to say

Never say "Just be careful." It approves the hazard. Never say "I'll pretend I didn't see that." You did, and a later investigation will find that you did. Never threaten the workers or the subcontractor in the moment; it shifts the conversation to blame while the edge is still open. And never say "We'll make up the time somehow" as a way to soften the stop, because it tells the superintendent the schedule still outranks the edge. The schedule conversation comes later, separately.

The question behind the question

"We're two weeks behind" means, "Will you hold this against us, and will you pay for recovery?" Answer it later, in the schedule meeting, with the contract: recovery is discussed against the programme and the contract's terms, not traded against a guardrail. "Our plan allows controlled access zones" may mean, "Are you going to second-guess our safety plan?" The answer is no: you are asking the contractor to follow its own plan, which is exactly what the contract requires.

When to stay silent

Once you have said the hazard, the outcome and that you will wait, stop talking. Let the superintendent act. Do not narrate, do not lecture, do not explain the regulations on the slab. Silence while the guardrail goes back up communicates more than a speech. Stay silent too if the superintendent is irritated; respond to the work being made safe, not to the tone.

After the slab

Three things follow, all in writing. A short note to the general contractor, factual and without blame, recording what you saw and asking for the corrective action. A note to your own file, with time, location and who was present. And, at the next schedule meeting, a conversation about why material landings were being done at open edges: usually because the logistics plan did not provide a protected loading point, which is a planning problem, not a worker's moral failure. Fix the plan, and the hazard stops recurring. If your loan documents or your partnership require reporting of safety matters, follow them.

Holding your state

You will feel the pull to avoid conflict, especially when the job is behind and the superintendent is someone you need. Notice that pull and treat it as information: the stronger it is, the more the pressure is pushing toward the hazard. If your heart is racing, slow your speech and lower your voice rather than raising it. Breathing drills belong before the walk, while parked, not on the slab; check that with your doctor if you have any heart or breathing condition. Remember the frame you already know from operations: stopping is not failing. Carrying on into a known hazard is.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an owner who sees a hazard and says nothing, because the job is behind and the owner does not want to seem to interfere. That silence teaches the whole site that schedule outranks safety. The control is a stated owner's rule, known to everyone, that anyone may stop unsafe work, including the owner, and that a stop is never penalised.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner either says nothing, or swings to the other extreme and starts directing the crew's methods, rearranging guardrails and assigning tasks. The first leaves the hazard. The second takes on responsibility for the contractor's methods. Name the hazard, require the outcome, follow up in writing.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught "I'll confirm by Friday": commit to a dated follow-up instead of improvising in the moment. The slab is the one place where the immediate answer cannot wait, but everything after it, the corrective action, the logistics fix and the schedule discussion, should go exactly that way: written, dated and owned.

Recap

See the hazard, speak to the person who controls the work, name it exactly, require the outcome, leave the method, and wait until it is done. Keep the schedule conversation separate. Follow up in writing and fix the plan that created the hazard.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: six questions on construction safety, a Red Pen drill on a site-specific safety plan, and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I speak first to the person who controls the work, not to another employer's workers.
I name the hazard exactly and require the outcome, leaving the method to the contractor.
I warn workers directly if the danger is immediate and no supervisor is present.
I wait until the hazard is controlled before moving on.
I keep the schedule conversation separate from the stop.
I follow up every stop in writing, factually and without blame.
I look for the planning failure behind each recurring hazard.
My site has a known rule that anyone may stop unsafe work without penalty.
head: Field checklist
speak: When I see danger on my site, I act in the moment. On a hypothetical slab, two framers are at an open edge with the guardrail down and no tie-off, and the job is two weeks behind. I speak to the superintendent, not to the workers: those men are unprotected, work at that edge stops now until it is protected, you decide how, and I will wait here. That names the hazard, states the outcome and leaves the method to the contractor, which keeps me from directing its methods. If the danger were immediate and no supervisor were present, I would warn the workers myself. When the superintendent says they are nearly done and behind schedule, I say we will talk about the schedule afterwards, not at this edge. Then I stay silent while it is fixed. Afterwards, I write it up, factually, and find the planning failure behind it, usually a logistics plan with no protected loading point.
terms: Stop-work authority — the right, given by a site's rules or contract, for any person to stop work they believe is unsafe without penalty.
Controlled access zone — a defined area near an unprotected edge where only authorised, trained workers may work under specific controls set out in the safety plan.
Corrective action — the documented change made after a hazard or incident to stop it recurring, with an owner and a completion date.

hostile.q: You stopped my crew for twenty minutes on a job that's already two weeks late. Are you going to pay for that time?
hostile.a: No. The crew was at an unprotected edge with the guardrail down and no tie-off, which your own safety plan does not allow. The twenty minutes was the cost of following your plan. I do want to talk about the two weeks, and I will, at the schedule meeting against the programme and the contract. I would also like to see how the logistics plan will give you a protected loading point, so the edge doesn't have to open again.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 53 Review: Focus Four, Shared Duties, Hold Points and Honest Rates
summary: Six questions test the week's core ideas on construction safety: the Focus Four, the multi-employer policy, Rule 53, the money of an incident, the general duty and incident rates. A Red Pen drill on an excerpt from a hypothetical site-specific safety plan, then a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: safety is decided before the site opens, by who you hire, what the contract requires and how much time the job has, and on site it is held by hold points, honest records and the willingness to stop.

Recall

Q. On the week's hypothetical numbers, what did a three-week stoppage cost before fines and repairs?

A. About 220,000 dollars: about 60,577 dollars of interest, 90,000 dollars of site overhead and about 69,231 dollars of delayed income.

Q. Why should an estimate at completion always carry its forecast method?

A. Because each formula assumes something about the future, such as remaining work at budget or at today's efficiency, and the reader needs the assumption to judge the number.

Q. What is the difference between a refinance and a take-out loan?

A. A take-out loan is committed in advance to repay the construction loan once stated conditions are met; a refinance is arranged later in the market, on whatever terms are then available.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, of all the subjects in this phase, this is the one where a failure is measured in lives, not dollars. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can prequalify a contractor, read a safety plan and handle a stop on site as an owner who knows his role. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the Focus Four, and say why they matter to a safety plan.

Answer: Falls, struck-by, caught-in or caught-between, and electrocution. Because the harm concentrates in them, a plan should name this site's exposure to each and the control for each, rather than spreading effort evenly.

Question 2. What are the four employer roles in OSHA's multi-employer citation policy, and how can an owner be drawn in?

Answer: Creating, exposing, correcting and controlling employer. An owner whose representatives direct how work is done, rather than what the result must be, may take on a controlling role for that hazard.

Question 3. State Rule 53.

Answer: Never let a structure, permanent or temporary, carry a load until a measured result shows it can; write that hold point into the plan, and never let schedule override it.

Question 4. Why are most of the costs of a serious incident uninsured?

Answer: Because insurance largely covers the direct costs, treatment and wage replacement, while the stopped site, investigation, repairs, legal costs, fines, late income and reputational harm usually fall on the project.

Question 5. What does the general duty in the federal safety law add to the specific standards?

Answer: It requires employers to keep workplaces free of recognised hazards likely to cause death or serious harm, so the absence of a specific standard is not a defence.

Question 6. Calculate the total recordable incident rate for 4 cases in 100,000 hours, and say why it beats comparing counts.

Answer: 4 times 200,000 divided by 100,000 equals 8.0. A rate adjusts for the hours worked, so a small firm with few cases can be seen to be much less safe than a large firm with more.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Duke set out the Focus Four, the multi-employer site, the site-specific safety plan, the job hazard analysis and safety prequalification. Ford and Cole took the Willow Island cooling tower collapse of 1978, where 51 workers died on a scaffold anchored to concrete not yet strong enough, giving Rule 53. Roman priced an incident and showed how safety records are priced into bids. REGA outlined Part 1926, the general duty, citations, and the Canadian and Guyanese approaches. Duke turned injury logs into rates and exposed the small-sample trap. Then he ran the stop-work conversation at an open edge.

The Red Pen

Read this excerpt from a hypothetical site-specific safety plan. Find the defects before reading on.

Section 4, Fall Protection. Fall protection will be provided where required by regulation. Guardrails may be removed temporarily for material landing at the discretion of the foreman. Section 6, Concrete and Formwork. Forms will be stripped on day 3 after placement to maintain the cycle. Section 8, Emergency. In case of injury call the site office; nearest hospital: see attached map (from the previous project). Section 9, Subcontractors. Subcontractors are responsible for their own safety. Section 11, Reporting. Near misses need not be reported unless an injury results. Approved by: Project Manager.

The defects. First, section 4 says fall protection will be provided "where required by regulation," which names no edge, opening or method on this site; it is generic, not site-specific. Second, removing guardrails "at the discretion of the foreman" for material landing is exactly the hazard on Day 6, with no controlled access zone, monitor or alternative protection required. Third, section 6 strips forms on a fixed day "to maintain the cycle," the Willow Island failure in miniature: stripping must follow a measured strength result and a named person's release, never a calendar. Fourth, the emergency section uses a map from a previous project, so in an emergency the route may be wrong; it also gives no address, no emergency number procedure and no responsible person. Fifth, "subcontractors are responsible for their own safety" ignores the general contractor's role as controlling employer and its duty to coordinate the site. Sixth, saying near misses need not be reported throws away the main leading indicator Duke taught on Day 5. Seventh, the plan is approved by the project manager alone, with no qualified safety professional named.

The corrected plan would name each exposed edge and its protection, require a planned, protected loading point or a controlled access zone with a monitor, tie stripping to field-cured cylinder or maturity results released by the temporary works engineer, give this site's emergency address and route, set out how the general contractor coordinates and inspects subcontractors, require near-miss reporting without penalty, and carry a safety professional's sign-off.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to an investor who asks, "How do you make sure nobody gets hurt on your sites?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Nobody can promise that, but we decide most of it before the site opens. We prequalify contractors on several years of injury rates per hours worked, their experience rating, citations and leading indicators like near-miss reporting, because a low price from a poor record is a cost we haven't been billed for yet. The contract requires a truly site-specific safety plan that names our falls, crane lifts, trenches and power lines, the four hazards that cause most deaths, and a hazard analysis before every high-risk task. Temporary works, formwork and scaffolds, are designed, and nothing carries a load until a test shows it can. We give the job enough time to plan safely. On site, anyone may stop unsafe work, including me, and when I see a hazard I tell the contractor's supervisor the outcome I need and let them fix it, so we don't take over their methods. And a serious incident would cost far more uninsured money than prevention does."

Score your own answer before comparing. Did you open with the bottom line? Did you name the Focus Four and Rule 53? Did you mention rates, not counts? Did you finish inside two minutes? If you missed any, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a safety plan that has every heading and describes no site, approved by someone without the training to see the gap. The control is to read the fall protection, formwork and emergency sections yourself and to require a safety professional's sign-off.

The beginner's mistake

Treating safety as the contractor's department and the owner's role as paying for it. The owner's choices on contractor, contract, time and money set the conditions every worker on site lives with.

Callback

In Week 48, Marco built the owner's decision log and approval authorities. Safety belongs in both: who may approve a deviation from the safety plan, and a dated record of every stop and its corrective action. A log that records cost decisions but not safety decisions shows a lender or a court exactly what the owner thought mattered.

Recap

Prequalify on rates, not counts. Require a site-specific plan built around the Focus Four, task-level hazard analysis and designed temporary works. Hold loads until a measured result releases them, as Rule 53 says. Monitor without directing methods, stop unsafe work at once, and follow up in writing.

head: The six questions
speak: Construction safety is decided before the site opens. OSHA's Focus Four, falls, struck-by, caught-in or between, and electrocution, cause most construction deaths, so my contractor's site-specific plan must name this site's exposure to each and the control for each. On a multi-employer site, the creating, exposing, correcting and controlling employer can all be cited, and an owner who directs methods can be drawn in, so I require outcomes and leave methods to the contractor. Rule 53, from the Willow Island collapse of 1978: nothing carries a load until a measured result shows it can. Most of an incident's cost is uninsured: a stopped site, interest, overhead and late income. The general duty means no specific rule is not a defence. I prequalify on rates, cases times 200,000 divided by hours, over several years, with leading indicators. And on site, anyone may stop unsafe work, including me.
terms: Site-specific safety plan — the general contractor's written plan for one site, naming its hazards, controls, emergency procedures and responsibilities.
Near miss — an event that could have caused injury or damage but did not, reported so its cause can be fixed.
Temporary works engineer — the qualified person responsible for designing temporary works, such as formwork and shoring, and for stating when they may be loaded or removed.

hostile.q: Your contractor's safety plan says forms come off on day 3 to keep the cycle. Isn't that efficient planning?
hostile.a: It is efficient until the day the concrete is not ready. Strength gain depends on temperature and mix, not on the calendar, and Willow Island showed what happens when a cycle decides when concrete can carry load. I will require the plan to tie stripping and reshoring to field-cured cylinder or maturity results, released in writing by the temporary works engineer. In warm weather that may still be day 3. In cold weather it will not be.
